summary: A 40-foot fire tower on Stone Mountain's summit was staffed by towerman Inez Shubert, as 1958 and 1963 newspaper reports describe.

facts.agency: Georgia State Forestry Service (named in the January 1958 report)

access.note: The summit is reached by a walk-up trail or the Skyride tram in Stone Mountain Park, which the state of Georgia owns. No source says whether the fire tower itself can be visited.

visit.trail_note: Walk-up trail on the west side of the mountain, or the Skyride aerial tram

events.note: Inez Shubert, a three-year veteran, worked as a towerman for the Georgia State Forestry Service (January 1958 report)
December 1963 report: Shubert, 36, a fire spotter whose office was the fire tower
National Geodetic Survey recovery note mentions an observation tower on the summit; the note does not identify it as the fire tower

evidence.supports: Stone Mountain is about nine miles east-northeast of Decatur
evidence.quote: THE STATION IS LOCATED 9 MILES EAST-NORTHEAST OF DECATUR

evidence.supports: Stone Mountain is a bare granite peak
evidence.quote: A WELL KNOWN BARE GRANITE PEAK

evidence.supports: By January 1958 a 40-foot tower stood on the summit; the lookout climbed it to watch for fires
evidence.quote: climbs to the top of the 40-foot tower to watch for forest fires

evidence.supports: Shubert was a towerman for the Georgia State Forestry Service
evidence.quote: She is a 'towerman' for the Georgia State Forestry Service

evidence.supports: Three-year veteran who could just about ignore the tower swaying
evidence.quote: A three-year veteran, she reports she is just about able to ignore the swaying of the tower

evidence.supports: One of the few women to hold such a position in the United States
evidence.quote: one of the few women to hold such a position in the United States

evidence.supports: Radio, heater and telephone as the comforts of home
evidence.quote: a radio, a heater and a telephone

evidence.supports: The 1958 report was carried by the Independent, Long Beach, California
December 1963: Shubert, 36, a fire spotter; her office was the fire tower
evidence.quote: is a fire spotter and her office is the fire tower on top of the world's largest mountain

evidence.supports: The 1963 report is credited to The Kansas City Times
Jeep drive except when rain or ice covers the ground
evidence.quote: Every day, except when it rains or ice covers the ground, Mrs. Shubert embarks in her jeep

evidence.supports: Sheer face impassable; trail up the backside
evidence.quote: The sheer face of Stone mountain is impassable, but Mrs. Shubert drives up the trail on the backside
RECOVERY NOTE BY NATIONAL GEODETIC SURVEY 1973

evidence.supports: Survey station 202 feet north of an observation tower on the summit
evidence.quote: 202 FEET NORTH OF THE NORTH SIDE OF THE OBSERVATION TOWER

evidence.supports: Aaron Cloud built a 165-foot wooden observation tower at the summit in 1838
evidence.quote: Entrepreneur Aaron Cloud built a 165 foot (50 m) wooden observation tower at the summit of the mountain in 1838

evidence.supports: A storm destroyed it; a much smaller tower replaced it in 1851
evidence.quote: it was destroyed by a storm and replaced by a much smaller tower in 1851

evidence.supports: Stone Mountain Park opened on April 14, 1965
evidence.quote: Stone Mountain Park officially opened on April 14, 1965

evidence.supports: The park is owned by the state of Georgia today
evidence.quote: The park today is owned by the state of Georgia

evidence.supports: The summit can be reached by a walk-up trail or the Skyride aerial tram
evidence.quote: The summit of the mountain can be reached by a walk-up trail on the west side of the mountain or by the Skyride aerial tram

notes_for_editor: Staffing (1958, 1963) is firm: the newspaper items are quoted on the Eastern US Lookouts page, and I did not reach the original newspapers. No source I reached gives the fire tower's build date, height beyond the 40-foot figure, or its fate. The 1973 NGS note's observation tower may or may not be the 1958 fire tower; the 1838 and 1851 towers were earlier tourist structures. Access is inferred from the Wikipedia summit route and the state ownership of the park; the fire tower itself is not described, so check the access and visit notes before publishing. The record's county is null and was not filled; the Wikipedia text I read does not name a county for the summit itself. The record's status is unknown and no status was added.
